title: Letter Workshop
idea: A quiet writing desk where support recedes as the child's own marks take over. The letter is the learning object; decoration never competes with its strokes.
visual: Warm ruled paper, ink-blue strokes, a small starting dot and a translucent guide. Feedback overlays the child's actual path rather than replacing it with a perfect letter.
core: Trace one letter with captured strokes. Introduce copy and independent formation as separate follow-up tasks.
reuse: Extend the existing LetterTracing displays into evaluated practice; inspect number/shape tracing for reusable pointer capture. Letter references and scoring remain new work.
prompts: Start at the dot. Trace lowercase l.
Make your own lowercase l beside the model.
Write lowercase l. The model is hidden.
student: Draw with a finger, stylus or mouse; clear and try again without losing the record of the first attempt.
feedback: After submission, compare the captured path with the reference. Show one useful correction, such as the starting point; keep assisted and independent attempts distinct.
mask: Independent writing removes letter forms, arrows and trace overlays. A spoken letter name is legitimate; showing its form is assistance.
evidence: Capture stroke order, start points, pen lifts, path coverage, case and assistance state. Establish tolerances from reviewed letter templates and learner trials; drawing near any line must not automatically pass.

variants.treatment: Uppercase and lowercase s, a, t, i, p, n; introduce trace, then separately check independent formation.
Introduce c, k, e, h, r, m, d while sampling the full cumulative 13-letter set.
Introduce g, o, u, l, f, b and retain review across all 19 letters.
Introduce j, z, w, v, y, x, q; preserve all 26 letters and both cases in the practice pool.

title: The Help Desk
idea: A friendly partner has information the child actually needs. A useful question changes the scene, giving conversation a purpose beyond filling a microphone turn.
visual: A small parcel counter, two possible destinations and a sealed information card. The partner's reply opens only the information the child asked for.
core: Ask one clarification question, hear the answer and use it in a second turn.
reuse: New bounded conversation primitive using existing audio infrastructure. A closed-answer DI pack cannot judge an original question or its follow-up.
prompts: Please deliver this parcel. What do you need to know?
The child asks: Who is it for?
It is for the rabbit. Tell your partner where you will take it.
student: Form a question aloud, listen to the specific reply, then explain or choose the next action.
feedback: The partner answers a relevant question naturally. For an unrelated question, preserve the missing information and prompt the child to reconsider what would help.
mask: Hide the recipient before the question; do not print a sentence for the child to repeat. Do not reward microphone use alone.
evidence: Retain question, relevance judgment, reply and follow-up. Accept alternative useful questions; test clarifying questions that are grammatically different but serve the same purpose.

variants.treatment: Alternate asking for help and answering a partner's help question.
Vary the missing detail: who, where, when or what; require a question that resolves that specific uncertainty.
Follow-up task: replace the parcel with a child's short presentation and support relevant audience questions in both directions.

title: Opinion Circle
idea: A small discussion table gives each child a viewpoint. Reasons accumulate beside the chosen story; there is no teacher-preferred opinion to guess.
visual: Two illustrated book covers, a chosen-book stand and blank reason pebbles. A second voice can offer a different view without a red wrong-answer state.
core: State a story preference and supply one relevant reason.
reuse: New response contract over story-talk/book context. Reuse story presentation; add opinion, rationale and peer-response evidence.
prompts: Which story would you hear again?
I like the garden story because the friends help each other.
Your partner likes the journey story. Do you agree? Tell them why.
student: Choose, speak a complete preference statement and explain it; later agree or disagree respectfully with a partner.
feedback: Reflect the child's reason and ask for a missing connection. Disagreement is welcome; an irrelevant reason receives a specific follow-up.
mask: Keep book references visible. Do not prefill reasons or label one preference as correct.
evidence: Record completeness, reason relevance, distinctness of multiple reasons and reference to the partner's view. Peer interaction still needs a real peer or observed classroom evidence.

variants.treatment: One I like statement with one story-grounded reason.
Add multiple distinct reasons; repeating the same reason does not fill another evidence slot.
Follow-up peer turn with complete agreement/disagreement and a reason; an AI partner is rehearsal, not proof of peer performance.

title: Show & Share
idea: A miniature presentation space with two objects and a few movable planning pictures. The audience listens while the child owns the floor.
visual: Two object plinths, a simple picture plan and a quiet recording indicator. No transcript teleprompter or ticking countdown.
core: Deliver a short focused description; build the two-object comparison as a subsequent task.
reuse: New presentation capture and rubric over existing media/audio. A sequence of short recall items cannot establish sustained presentation.
prompts: What could you tell us about a ball and a block?
Tell how they are alike and different.
Listen to your ideas. What would you make clearer?
student: Arrange a few picture reminders, present aloud, then review a recorded section with a teacher or tutor.
feedback: Use actual excerpts to discuss clarity and focus. Recording volume alone cannot establish whether a classroom audience heard the child.
mask: Keep planning objects visible but do not supply a completed script. Measure duration silently rather than displaying time pressure.
evidence: Retain duration, source audio, topic continuity and comparison evidence. Classroom audibility requires observation; the two-minute requirement needs an actual sustained recording.

variants.treatment: Collect an audible classroom sharing observation; microphone rehearsal is supporting evidence only.
A focused two-minute comparison with both objects referenced; silent duration measurement and a teacher-reviewable recording.

title: Action Stage
idea: The child becomes a director and performer. A short action card changes how a movement is performed, making verbs and adverbs observable.
visual: An open floor, a simple actor silhouette and a director card. Motion trails demonstrate pace only during modeling, then disappear for the child's turn.
core: Give and follow one familiar action instruction with an adult observer.
reuse: New observed activity contract; existing spatial scenes may illustrate the instruction but cannot verify off-screen child movement.
prompts: Wave slowly.
Your turn. Show what slowly changes.
Give your partner a different action to follow.
student: Perform an action physically, then give a partner an original command; an observer records what actually happened.
feedback: Compare the performed action with the requested manner. Offer a model after an attempt, with movement and voice alternatives appropriate to the child.
mask: Remove the demonstration during the independent action. An animated avatar completing the direction is not evidence that the child performed it.
evidence: Separate spoken command quality from observed movement. Record observer confirmation and accommodations; do not infer physical performance from button clicks.

variants.treatment: Contrast quickly/slowly through movement and loudly through an appropriate voice activity; record the relevant observed manner.
Alternate following and giving familiar classroom commands, capturing both roles.

title: You & Me
idea: Two partners trade roles in a familiar routine. Pronouns change with the speaker, so the same scene cannot be solved by memorizing a fixed label.
visual: Two facing activity mats, a speaker token and a shared task such as packing a bag. The speaking position is always clear.
core: Describe an action using I or you from the current speaker's perspective.
reuse: New perspective-sensitive oral task; reuse scene rendering and audio while adding actor, speaker and referent tracking.
prompts: You packed your own bag. Tell your partner.
I packed my bag myself.
Now your partner is speaking. Who does you refer to?
student: Speak about their own or the partner's action, then switch roles and adjust the pronoun.
feedback: Highlight the current speaker and actor after a referent error; model the sentence from that perspective.
mask: Show roles and actions, but hide the model sentence until feedback. Colors must not permanently encode I and you.
evidence: Judge speaker, actor and referent together, accepting natural alternative sentences. Routine use needs observed transfer beyond the pictured rehearsal.

variants.treatment: Alternate I/you during familiar routines and conversations; preserve which participant is speaking.
Follow-up reflexive task: myself/yourself must refer back to the actor rather than merely appear in the utterance.

title: Story Ribbon
eyebrow: Connect a story to your world
idea: A ribbon of pictured moments turns disconnected words into a connected account. A second ribbon can hold the child's own experience beside the story.
visual: Three spacious event frames with an optional time cue; a personal-experience card sits alongside rather than being forced into the fictional sequence.
core: Tell a connected account of three pictured events.
reuse: Extend story-planner with original spoken narration and recorded evidence; ordering cards alone remains planning evidence.
prompts: The child planted a seed, watered it and saw a sprout.
Tell this story as something that happened yesterday.
Does this remind you of something you have done?
student: Arrange pictures, narrate an original account and connect a story event to an experience when requested.
feedback: Replay a short excerpt, then prompt a missing event link or inconsistent time reference. Allow the child to decline a personal disclosure and use another familiar experience.
mask: Keep event pictures visible; hide scripted narration. Time cues can be legitimate support but must not supply conjugated answers.
evidence: Capture temporal consistency, linked events and the explicit story-to-experience connection. Do not grade the truth or emotional value of a personal memory.

variants.treatment: Follow-up tense tasks: present, past and future story contexts, judged consistently rather than by one exact sentence.
Connect one identified story event to a personal or familiar experience and explain the connection.

title: Puppet Studio
idea: A tiny stage lets the child move characters and author their voices. The performance—not selecting a character card—is the response.
visual: A simple curtain, two large movable puppets and a scene prop. A speaking halo follows the active puppet; recorded turns appear as small replay beads.
core: Create a two-turn exchange between two characters.
reuse: Extend story-planner/scene assets with performance capture. New synchronized puppet movement, actor identity and voice-turn evidence are required.
prompts: Rabbit and Bear find one umbrella in the rain.
What does Rabbit say?
What might Bear say back?
student: Choose and move a puppet, speak an original line, switch character and produce a connected reply.
feedback: Replay the exchange with puppet movement. Discuss whether the reply connects to the first line; preserve creative alternatives.
mask: Keep character and scene cues visible; hide model dialogue. Voice imitation deliberately allows a model because imitation is the assessed action.
evidence: Record speaker-labeled turns and movement. Assess connected dialogue separately from imitation or story-detail enactment; never use accent conformity as a success criterion.

variants.treatment: Two-character dialogue with connected, child-authored turns.
Separate imitation task: replay a familiar read-aloud character, then capture an expressive imitation for review.
Enact a supplied story's main idea and details; movement/puppetry needs actual performance evidence, not a selected scene.

title: Word Garden
idea: Picture ideas grow into a network the child constructs. Each line has a meaning; the garden metaphor follows the relationship rather than rewarding arbitrary decoration.
visual: A spacious mat with movable picture seeds, a theme in the middle and soft connecting stems. Unused distractors remain outside the web.
core: Build a thematic web with three or four related picture nodes.
reuse: New semantic-links interaction. Reuse generic node/drag utilities if available; spelling chains and chronological arcs do not supply semantic link judgments.
prompts: Make a farm word garden.
Connect cow, barn and hay to your theme.
Tell why hay belongs with the cow.
student: Place and link pictures, then explain a relationship. Multiple defensible networks are welcome.
feedback: Respond to an individual link, not the overall prettiness. Ask about a doubtful connection before rejecting it.
mask: Do not preconnect correct nodes or encode correct links by position/color. Reveal example relationships only after the attempt.
evidence: Store nodes, edges and relation explanations. A later chain task additionally requires meaningful directed adjacent links; thematic membership alone cannot certify a chain.

variants.treatment: Three or four related items connected to a theme with distractors and more than one defensible web.
Follow-up directed chain: seed to plant to flower to bee; judge each adjacent logical connection, not spelling or chronology alone.

title: Scene Speaker
idea: A detailed but readable scene invites an original sentence. Vocabulary tiles are ingredients, not a preassembled sentence to imitate.
visual: One large illustration and a small bank of audible pictured words. A child's recorded sentence becomes a replay card beside the scene.
core: Describe a pictured event in one original complete sentence.
reuse: New open-sentence response contract over existing picture vocabulary/scene assets. The closed single-word frame remains useful but does not prove sentence production.
prompts: A child in boots jumps into a puddle beside a dog.
Tell what is happening. Try using boots and splash.
Listen to your sentence. What else could your listener learn?
student: Inspect the scene, hear vocabulary if needed and produce a sentence without arranging a supplied model.
feedback: Reflect meaning and ask for one missing element. Accept different valid descriptions rather than matching a single transcript.
mask: Vocabulary words are allowed scaffolding; a complete example sentence stays hidden until feedback. Record whether the word bank was used.
evidence: Capture sentence completeness, scene fidelity and meaningful use of the requested vocabulary. Repeating disconnected bank words is not sentence evidence.

variants.treatment: Vary familiar people, places, things and events, checking complete descriptive sentences.
Require multiple bank words used meaningfully in the scene description; retain valid paraphrases.

title: Idea Canopy
idea: A main idea sits above the details that support it. The child builds the structure from a story they heard, so every link can point back to evidence.
visual: A broad idea card at the top, three detail spaces underneath and a tray containing a related but unstated distractor. The hierarchy stays visible without preplacing answers.
core: Choose a supplied main idea and attach supporting picture details from one read-aloud.
reuse: New passage-grounded organizer or substantial extension of story-map. Generic sorting lacks the shared story evidence required for these judgments.
steps: Check a detail against the story
prompts: Mina planted seeds, watered them each day and watched sprouts grow.
Which pictures support Mina cared for her plants?
Was picking an apple in this story, or is it only related to gardens?
student: Place the main idea and supporting details, then inspect the source for a questionable link.
feedback: Replay the supporting story excerpt after submission; distinguish an unstated detail from a false one.
mask: Shuffle answer cards and keep source text accessible by audio. Do not reveal the completed hierarchy before the attempt.
evidence: Store role assignments, support links and source references. Follow-up tasks can sort idea/detail roles and distribute details across several main ideas.

variants.treatment: Separate role-sorting task: classify picture cards as main idea or supporting detail, with a shared story.
Build a web connecting the selected main idea to its supporting details.
Follow-up multiple-idea workspace: match each detail to the corresponding main idea and retain the links.

title: Story Bridge
idea: Two stories remain open on facing shores. Children build bridges between meaningful similarities and keep differences anchored to the story they came from.
visual: Two compact illustrated story panels, a shared middle area and movable character, setting or event cards. A Venn overlay is introduced only for that explicit task.
core: Match a similar character across two supplied stories and explain the connection.
reuse: Extend story-talk/story-map to retain two source contexts and cross-story evidence. Single-story recall does not establish comparison.
prompts: Rabbit shares an umbrella. Fox shares a blanket.
Find what the two characters have in common.
Both share something to help a friend. How are their situations different?
student: Match or place evidence from both stories, then describe the relationship aloud where required.
feedback: Bring the two relevant story excerpts together. Accept supported alternatives; do not confuse visual resemblance with similar character behavior.
mask: Keep both sources available, but hide completed bridges and similarity labels. Avoid matching solely by identical card colors.
evidence: Store the source of each selected card and the relation asserted. Distinct follow-up contracts handle settings, difference statements, main ideas, Venn placement and event sequences.

variants.treatment: Match similar characters using pictures and behavior evidence from both stories.
Separate setting-matching task with source-labeled setting cards.
Produce a spoken similarity statement, not just a successful match.
Produce a spoken difference grounded in the two characters.
Follow-up teacher-guided Venn surface with explicit shared and story-specific regions.
Follow-up two-lane event sequences preserving order within each story before comparison.
Compare each story's main idea with visual evidence and guided discussion; character matching alone does not satisfy this.
